Dear Ms Thornton,

I am writing to express my concern about the proposed closure of the school library. While I understand that budget pressures require difficult decisions, I believe closing the library would be a serious mistake.

The library is not simply a room full of books. It is the only quiet space in the school where students can work without distraction. It is where Year 11 students revise during free periods. It is where students who do not have internet access at home complete their homework. Removing it would disproportionately affect the students who need the most support.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss alternative cost-saving measures with you.

Yours sincerely,
Jamie Okonkwo

passages.text:
Why Your Bike Could Be Your Best GCSE Revision Tool

Every morning, hundreds of students arrive at the school gates having spent thirty minutes sealed inside a car or crammed onto a bus, headphones in, eyes glazed. They shuffle into registration already tired. But a small number arrive differently — alert, awake, slightly out of breath — because they cycled.

The science is not complicated. Exercise increases blood flow to the brain, which improves concentration and memory. A 2022 study from the University of Edinburgh found that students who exercised before school scored an average of twelve per cent higher in concentration tests than those who did not. Cycling is not just transport. It is a free, daily dose of the thing every revision guide tells you to do more of: physical activity.

So before you spend another twenty pounds on highlighters and flashcards, consider this: your best revision tool might already be rusting in the garage.

Good evening, parents, teachers, and governors.

I want to talk to you tonight about something that does not appear on any exam paper but affects every result your children bring home: their mental health.

We tell students to work harder, revise longer, aim higher. We mean well. But we rarely ask them how they are coping. A survey conducted in this school last term found that sixty-eight per cent of Year 11 students described their stress levels as high or very high. Forty-one per cent said they had lost sleep over exams in the previous week. These are not statistics from a government report. These are your children.

Some will say that pressure is part of life — that learning to cope with stress is itself a valuable skill. And they are right, to a point. But there is a difference between productive challenge and chronic overwhelm. When a student stops eating breakfast because revision has consumed their morning, we have crossed a line.

What I am asking for tonight is not less ambition. It is more honesty. Let us talk to students about stress as openly as we talk about grades. Let us build five minutes of breathing exercises into every revision session. Let us stop pretending that wellbeing and achievement are opposites — because the evidence shows they are partners.

Thank you.

passages.text:
Time to Fix the Canteen

Every lunchtime, six hundred students have forty minutes to eat. By the time most reach the front of the queue, twenty of those minutes have gone. What arrives on the tray is lukewarm pasta or a sandwich that bends like cardboard.

The problem is not the kitchen staff, who work hard with limited resources. The problem is the system. One serving hatch for six hundred students is not a staffing issue — it is a design failure. Other schools in the area have introduced a pre-order app that cuts queue times in half. Ours has not.

If the school is serious about student wellbeing, it should start with the meal that fuels the afternoon.

passages.text:
I Deleted Social Media for a Month. Here Is What Actually Happened.

I expected withdrawal symptoms. I expected to feel isolated, out of the loop, socially invisible. I expected to cave within a week. None of that happened.

What happened instead was quieter and stranger. I started noticing things: the colour of the sky on the walk to school, the conversations I had been half-listening to while scrolling, the fact that I could read for thirty minutes without reaching for my phone. I slept better. I argued less with my parents. My homework took less time — not because there was less of it, but because I actually did it instead of pretending to.

I am not going to tell you to delete your accounts. That kind of advice is easy to give and impossible to follow. But I will say this: the version of my life that existed without social media was not smaller. It was, in almost every measurable way, larger.

passages.text:
The Park That Built a Community Is Being Left to Rot

Willow Green Park has served this town for over forty years. Generations of children have learned to ride bikes on its paths. Teenagers have revised for exams on its benches. Elderly residents have walked its circuit every morning since retirement. It is, by any measure, the most used public space in the borough.

And yet, the council's draft budget for next year proposes cutting its maintenance funding by sixty per cent. The flower beds, already patchy, would go unplanted. The playground equipment, some of which has not been replaced since 2009, would receive no safety inspections. The single public toilet would close permanently.

The council argues that parks are a luxury in an era of shrinking budgets. But a park is not a luxury — it is infrastructure. It is the place where isolated pensioners meet their only social contact of the day. It is where new parents find community. It is where teenagers go when they have nowhere else. Cutting its budget does not save money. It transfers the cost — to the NHS, to social services, to the police — and it makes it invisible.

Willow Green Park does not need a campaign. It needs a council that can tell the difference between expenditure and investment.

Dear Mrs Kapoor,

I am writing to request that the school reconsiders its uniform policy, specifically the requirement for blazers to be worn at all times during the summer term.

Last June, classroom temperatures regularly exceeded twenty-eight degrees. Students in full blazers struggled to concentrate, and several reported headaches by mid-afternoon. The science block, which has no air conditioning, was particularly affected. Allowing students to remove blazers in warm weather would cost the school nothing and would improve comfort, concentration, and wellbeing.

I understand that uniform promotes a sense of identity and discipline. I am not suggesting it be abandoned — only that a common-sense exception be made when the weather demands it.

I would be grateful if this could be discussed at the next student council meeting.

Yours sincerely,
Aisha Begum

Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to last week's article about the decline of our high street. Your reporter blamed online shopping and rising rents. These are real factors, but they are not the whole story. Walk down Greenfield Road on any Saturday morning and the first thing you notice is not the empty shops — it is the litter.

Coffee cups line the gutter. Fast food wrappers sit in doorways. A bin was removed from outside the post office three months ago and has never been replaced. The message this sends to visitors, shoppers, and potential business owners is simple: nobody cares about this place.

I do not believe the solution is more signs telling people not to litter. People already know. The solution is infrastructure: more bins, more frequent collections, and a council that treats cleanliness as an economic investment, not a cosmetic expense.

Yours faithfully,
Daniel Osei

Dear Councillor Whitfield,

I understand that the council faces a budget shortfall of two point three million pounds and that difficult decisions must be made. I am writing, however, to argue that closing the Meadowbank Youth Centre should not be one of them.

The centre serves over two hundred young people each week. For many, it is the only safe, supervised space available to them outside school. It provides homework support, mental health drop-ins, and a basketball court that is used every evening until nine. Closing it would not simply remove a service — it would remove a lifeline.

You may argue that youth services are discretionary spending. Technically, that is correct. But discretionary does not mean dispensable. The youth centre costs the council approximately forty-five thousand pounds per year. A single anti-social behaviour prosecution — the kind that rises sharply when youth provision disappears — costs an average of eight thousand. The maths is not complicated.

I recognise that budgets are finite. But I would ask you to consider what kind of borough you want this to be: one that invests in young people before they need intervention, or one that pays for the consequences of not doing so.

Yours sincerely,
Sophia Mensah

There is a moment in the second act of Thornfield Academy's production of Blood Brothers where the lighting shifts to a cold blue, and the audience falls completely silent. It lasts perhaps five seconds. In those five seconds, this stops being a school play.

The production is not flawless. Some scene transitions feel rushed, and the sound levels in the opening number drown out the lyrics. But these are minor complaints in a show that gets the big things right: the performances are committed, the staging is inventive, and the final scene lands with genuine emotional weight.

If you missed it, you missed something worth seeing. And if you think school plays are just awkward singing and forgotten lines, this one would have changed your mind.

passages.text:
Marco's on Church Street does not look like much from the outside. The sign is peeling. The menu in the window has yellowed at the edges. You walk past it on the way to somewhere that looks more promising. That is your first mistake.

Inside, the dining room is small and unpretentious — maybe twelve tables, paper napkins, no background music. The menu is short: pasta, risotto, two fish dishes, and whatever Marco feels like making that day. Our waiter recommended the aubergine parmigiana, and I have not stopped thinking about it since.

The pasta is made fresh. You can see it through the kitchen hatch — Marco rolling dough at a speed that suggests he has been doing this for decades, which he has. The tagliatelle with slow-cooked lamb was rich without being heavy, the kind of dish that makes you eat slowly because you do not want it to end.

Marco's will not win any awards for ambience. The chairs are mismatched. The bill arrives handwritten on a receipt pad. But the food is honest, generous, and cooked with the kind of care that chain restaurants spend millions trying to imitate. Go on a Tuesday when it is quiet. Order the parmigiana. Thank me later.
passages.label: Model B — Review of a local restaurant

passages.text:
The producers of Breathing Room had a simple question: what happens to a teenager's mental health when you remove their phone for thirty days? The answer, filmed across six months with eight volunteers from a London comprehensive, is more complicated — and more moving — than any headline about screen addiction has managed to be.

The documentary resists the obvious narrative. It does not set out to prove that phones are bad. Instead, it watches. It watches Callum, fifteen, discover that he draws when he is bored — something he had not done since primary school. It watches Priya, sixteen, have her first uninterrupted conversation with her mother in months and not know what to say. It watches Leo hand back his phone on day thirty and immediately check how many followers he has lost.

What makes Breathing Room exceptional is its refusal to moralise. There are no experts in armchairs explaining dopamine. There are no statistics flashing across the screen. There is just the slow, uncomfortable truth of eight young people learning what their lives look like without a screen to hide behind.

The final ten minutes are devastating. Not because anything dramatic happens, but because nothing does. The teenagers return to their phones, and within a week, most of them are exactly where they started. The documentary does not judge them for it. It simply asks: is this enough?

Good morning, everyone.

I want to talk about something we all experience but nobody ever talks about: assemblies. Specifically, why most of them do not work.

Every week, we sit in rows and listen to someone read from a PowerPoint about resilience, or respect, or some other word that starts with R. We nod. We clap politely. We forget the whole thing by break time.

Assemblies could be different. They could be run by students. They could feature debates, spoken word, live demonstrations. They could be the one time in the week when this school actually listens to the people who fill its corridors.

I am not asking for less assemblies. I am asking for better ones. Because right now, we are wasting four hundred hours of collective attention every Monday morning. And attention is the one thing this school keeps telling us we should value.

Good evening.

I am sixteen years old. By the time I am old enough to vote, the decisions that will determine whether this town floods in twenty years will already have been made. By you. Tonight.

I am not here to lecture you about polar bears or melting ice caps. You have heard those arguments. You have nodded at those arguments. And then you have driven home and done nothing about them. So let me make this local.

Last winter, the river broke its banks on Meadow Lane for the third time in five years. Fourteen families were flooded. Three of them are still not back in their homes. The drainage infrastructure on that road has not been updated since 1987. This is not a global problem. This is a plumbing problem. And it is yours to fix.

I know what you are thinking: money. There is never enough. But flooding costs more than prevention. Every pound spent on drainage saves four in emergency services, temporary housing, and insurance claims. That is not idealism. That is arithmetic.

So here is what I am asking. Not a revolution. Not a protest. Just a drainage plan for Meadow Lane, funded by the emergency reserve that exists precisely for emergencies that keep happening. Because if you wait for the next flood to act, you are not governing. You are just watching.

Good evening, and thank you for coming.

I am here to argue something that might surprise you, coming from a student: that compulsory sport should stay on the timetable. Not because I enjoy it — I do not, particularly — but because the alternative is worse.

Let me explain. When people campaign to make sport optional, they imagine a world in which students who hate PE are finally free. But that is not what happens. What happens is that the students who already exercise keep exercising, and the students who do not stop moving entirely. The gap widens. The students who most need physical activity are the ones who opt out.

I know this because I am one of them. Left to my own devices, I would spend every free period sitting down. Compulsory sport is the only reason I move for forty minutes on a Wednesday afternoon. I do not love it. But I leave it feeling better than when I arrived. Every single time.

The objection I hear most often is choice. Students should be allowed to choose. And I agree — in principle. But choice requires information. A fourteen-year-old opting out of sport does not fully understand what they are giving up: the cardiovascular benefit, the stress reduction, the social connection that happens when you are too out of breath to be self-conscious.

So no, I am not asking you to make sport fun. I am asking you to keep it compulsory. Because some of the most important things we do are the things we would never choose to do on our own.

How to Revise Without Losing Your Mind

A guide for students who want to do well without burning out.

Start Early, Start Small
The biggest revision mistake is leaving everything until the last week. Instead, begin four to six weeks before your first exam. Start with just twenty minutes a day. Your brain learns better in short, regular sessions than in one desperate marathon.

Use Active Methods
Reading your notes is not revising. It feels productive, but very little sticks. Instead, try: covering your notes and writing what you remember, testing yourself with flashcards, or explaining a topic out loud to someone who knows nothing about it. If it feels easy, it is probably not working.

Take Breaks Seriously
A ten-minute break every forty-five minutes is not laziness — it is science. Your concentration drops sharply after about fifty minutes of focused work. Step away from your desk. Move. Drink water. Then come back.

You Do Not Need to Be Perfect
Revision is not about memorising every detail. It is about understanding enough to answer the question in front of you. Focus on the topics you find hardest, not the ones you already know. That is where the marks are.

Stay Visible. Stay Safe. A Quick Guide to Cycling on Roads.

You Already Know the Rules — Here Is Why They Matter

Every year in the UK, over two thousand cyclists under eighteen are injured on the roads. Most of those injuries happen in situations that are preventable: riding without lights at dusk, swerving without signalling, wearing headphones and missing the sound of a turning vehicle. This guide will not tell you to wrap yourself in cotton wool. It will give you three things to remember every time you get on a bike.

1. Be Seen Before You Are Hit
After October, daylight fades fast. Front and rear lights are a legal requirement after dark, but you should use them whenever visibility is poor — drizzle, fog, early morning. A reflective vest costs less than five pounds. It could save your life.

2. Signal Like You Mean It
A vague hand wave is not a signal. Extend your arm fully, hold it for three seconds, and check behind you before you move. Drivers are not mind readers. Give them time to react.

3. One Ear In, One Ear Out
We know you want to listen to music. Fine. But keep one ear free. The sound of a bus pulling out, a car door opening, or a pedestrian shouting is information your playlist cannot give you.

Ride Smart, Not Scared
Cycling is one of the best things you can do for your health, your independence, and the environment. These three habits do not make it less fun. They make sure you are around to enjoy it tomorrow.

passages.text:
When Everything Feels Like Too Much: A Honest Guide to Looking After Your Head

This guide is for you if you have ever felt overwhelmed, anxious, or low — and did not know what to do about it. You are not alone. One in six young people in the UK experiences a mental health difficulty. This is not a weakness. It is a fact.

Notice What You Feel
The first step is the hardest: admitting that something is wrong. You do not need a diagnosis. You do not need to explain it perfectly. If you have noticed that you feel different — more tired, more irritable, less interested in things you used to enjoy — that is enough to take seriously.

Talk to Someone You Trust
This does not have to be a parent or a teacher. It could be a friend, a sibling, a school counsellor, or an anonymous helpline. The point is to say it out loud. Thoughts that feel enormous inside your head often shrink the moment you share them.

Small Things, Consistently
Mental health is not fixed by one big gesture. It is maintained by small, boring habits: sleeping at roughly the same time each night, moving your body for twenty minutes a day, eating something that is not processed sugar, and spending time with people who make you feel calm.

Know When to Ask for More Help
If your feelings are affecting your sleep, your appetite, your friendships, or your ability to get through a school day, it is time to speak to a professional. This is not dramatic. This is sensible. Your GP, your school counsellor, or a service like Young Minds can help.

You Are Not Broken
Feeling bad does not mean you are bad. It means you are human, and you are paying attention. The fact that you are reading this guide is already a step in the right direction.

Dear Chair of Governors,

I am writing to raise concerns regarding the nutritional quality of the meals currently provided in the school canteen.

A significant proportion of the daily menu consists of processed items with limited nutritional value. Students who rely on school meals as their primary midday nutrition are not receiving adequate sustenance to maintain concentration throughout the afternoon. Research conducted by the Food Foundation in 2023 indicates that schools providing freshly prepared meals see measurable improvements in attendance and attainment.

I would respectfully request that the governing body reviews the current catering contract with a view to prioritising nutritional standards alongside cost efficiency.

Yours faithfully,
Raheem Chaudhry

Okay, Can We Talk About the Canteen?

I do not know who decided that a beige rectangle of breaded something counts as lunch, but I would like a word with them.

Look, I am not expecting restaurant-quality dining. I know this is a school, not a bistro. But when the healthiest option on the menu is a bruised apple and a carton of juice that expired yesterday, something has gone wrong.

Here is the thing: we spend six hours a day in this building. We are told to focus, to work hard, to achieve. And then at lunchtime we are handed a plate of chips and expected to power through double maths on that. It does not add up — and I say that as someone who struggles with maths at the best of times.

I am not asking for avocado toast and smoothie bowls. I am asking for food that does not make me want to sleep through Period 5.

passages.text:
Should School Start at Ten?

The science is clear. Teenagers' circadian rhythms shift during puberty, making it biologically difficult for them to fall asleep before eleven at night. Asking a fifteen-year-old to be alert at half past eight in the morning is, according to sleep researchers, the equivalent of asking an adult to perform at four in the morning.

Despite this, the vast majority of secondary schools in the UK still begin before nine. The reason is not educational — it is logistical. School times are built around bus timetables, parental work schedules, and after-school childcare. The needs of the students come last.

However, some schools have begun to experiment. In 2019, a comprehensive in Oxford moved its start time to ten o'clock for a one-year trial. Attendance improved. Behavioural incidents dropped. Students reported feeling less anxious. The school reverted to its original hours the following year — not because the trial failed, but because the bus company refused to adjust its routes.

This is the real obstacle. Not biology. Not evidence. Not even cost. Transport.

Until we are willing to redesign the systems around the students, rather than the other way around, we will continue to teach children who are half asleep — and then blame them for not paying attention.

passages.text:
Let me ask you something. How many of you are wearing something today that cost less than ten pounds?

Now let me ask you this: do you know who made it?

Fast fashion is built on a simple promise: you can look good for almost nothing. And for the consumer, it works. A five-pound T-shirt looks the same as a fifty-pound one. The fabric feels similar. The fit is fine. The problem is not what you see. It is what you do not.

Behind that five-pound T-shirt is a supply chain that begins in a cotton field in India and ends in a landfill in Ghana. Along the way, it passes through factories where workers earn less than two pounds an hour, dye houses that dump untreated chemicals into rivers, and shipping containers that cross three oceans burning fuel that nobody accounts for.

On the other hand, asking teenagers to boycott cheap clothing is unrealistic. Not everyone can afford to shop ethically. Not everyone has access to second-hand alternatives. The responsibility does not lie with you. It lies with the companies that profit from a system designed to be invisible.

Consequently, the question is not whether you should buy cheap clothes. The question is whether the companies that sell them should be allowed to hide where they come from. Transparency is not a luxury. It is the minimum we should demand.

Dear Editor,

Your recent editorial praised the rise in part-time employment among sixteen-year-olds, framing it as a sign of resilience and entrepreneurial spirit. I would like to offer an alternative reading.

It is true that part-time work can build confidence, teach time management, and provide financial independence. These are genuine benefits, and I do not dismiss them. Many students find that a Saturday job gives them a sense of purpose that school alone does not.

Nevertheless, the sharp increase in working hours among Year 11 students — up twenty-three per cent since 2020, according to the Sutton Trust — deserves scrutiny rather than celebration. A significant proportion of these students are not working for pocket money. They are working because their families need the income. They are filling shifts at supermarkets and fast food restaurants not to build a CV, but to keep the heating on.

Moreover, the impact on educational outcomes is well documented. Students who work more than twelve hours per week during term time are twice as likely to underperform in their GCSEs. The correlation between rising youth employment and falling GCSE attainment in deprived areas is not coincidental. It is causal.

I would therefore suggest that your editorial's optimism, while well intentioned, overlooks a troubling reality: for many young people, working is not a choice. It is a necessity imposed by poverty. Celebrating it without acknowledging this context risks normalising a situation that should concern us all.

Yours faithfully,
Nadia Kowalski

Our School Is Falling Apart. Nobody Seems to Care.

The ceiling in Room 14 has been leaking since September. The science block toilets have been out of order for three weeks. The heating in the English corridor works on alternate Tuesdays — or so it feels.

This is not a school in a disaster zone. This is a school in one of the wealthiest countries on earth. And yet our students are learning in conditions that would not be tolerated in a prison.

Who is responsible? The headteacher, who has submitted seven maintenance requests this term alone? The local authority, which has cut its building budget by forty per cent in five years? Or the government, which talks endlessly about world-class education while the world-class ceilings drip onto world-class exercise books?

Our students deserve better. Our teachers deserve better. Our community deserves better. The question is whether anyone in a position of power is willing to listen.

passages.text:
Good afternoon.

I want to talk about freedom. Not the abstract, philosophical kind — the practical kind. The kind that means a sixteen-year-old can get to a job interview without asking their parents for a lift. The kind that means a student in a rural village can attend an after-school club without being stranded at the bus stop until seven. The kind that a bus pass provides.

Public transport in this country is failing young people. Fares have risen thirty-one per cent in the last decade. Routes have been cut. Evening services have been slashed. In rural areas, some villages have no bus service at all. If you are sixteen and you do not have a parent with a car, your world is the size of your postcode.

Some will argue that subsidised transport is not affordable. I would argue that the alternative is more expensive. A young person who cannot access work, education, or social life does not disappear. They become isolated. They become disengaged. They become a cost to the system that a ten-pound bus pass would have prevented.

This is not about convenience. It is about equality. It is about giving every young person — not just those born within walking distance of a train station — the chance to build a life beyond their front door.

Dear Editor,

Last month, your newspaper published an editorial under the headline 'Generation Me: Why Today's Teenagers Only Think of Themselves.' I would like to challenge every word of that headline — starting with the assumption behind it.

The teenagers I know volunteer at food banks on Saturday mornings. They coach younger children in sports clubs without being paid. They organise charity fundraisers that raise thousands. They sit with elderly neighbours who have no one else to talk to. They do these things not for university applications or Instagram likes, but because they believe it matters.

Your headline does not just misrepresent young people. It discourages the very behaviour it claims to miss. When adults tell teenagers they are selfish, self-absorbed, and screen-addicted, what incentive do they have to prove otherwise? Mockery is not motivation. Contempt is not a call to action.

The real question is not whether teenagers care. It is whether the adults writing headlines about them have bothered to look. Because if they had — if they had spent one Saturday morning at the food bank on Cromwell Road, or one evening at the youth football club on Marsh Lane — they would have found their answer.

But that, of course, would require leaving the office.

Yours faithfully,
Eleanor Okafor

The Homework Myth

Homework is one of those things that everyone has an opinion about but nobody questions properly. Parents assume it is essential. Teachers set it because they always have. Students endure it because they have no choice. But what if the evidence does not support the habit?

A 2023 study by the University of Bath found that homework has a measurable impact on achievement only when it is purposeful, focused, and limited to thirty minutes per subject. Beyond that threshold, the returns diminish sharply. A student who spends three hours on homework each evening is not three times more prepared; they are simply three times more exhausted.

The semicolon in the previous sentence is doing important work. It links two related ideas without a full stop's hard break or a comma's breathless rush. That is what good punctuation does: it controls the reader's pace and clarifies meaning.

Teenagers and Charity: We Do More Than You Think

Every weekend, hundreds of teenagers across the country give up their free time to volunteer. They work in charity shops. They help at food banks. They raise money for causes they believe in. This is not because anyone forces them to. It is because they care.

Some adults seem surprised by this. They assume that teenagers care only about social media and video games — a stereotype that says more about the adults than the teenagers. Most young people I know want to make a difference; they simply lack the opportunity or the guidance.

Charity work gives teenagers a sense of purpose. It builds confidence, develops transferable skills, and introduces them to communities they might never otherwise encounter. Employers value volunteering on a CV; universities notice it too. If you have ever dismissed a teenager as lazy or self-obsessed, perhaps it is time to look again.

Good evening.

I would like to talk about something that every school values in its prospectus but cuts first when the budget tightens: the arts.

Drama, music, and art are not luxuries. They are the subjects where students who struggle academically discover that they are not, in fact, failures — they are creative, expressive, and capable of producing something that moves other people. Cut the arts, and you do not save money. You remove the one space in the timetable where a student who cannot pass a maths exam can feel like they matter.

The irony is exquisite. We talk about wellbeing in assemblies; we teach resilience through PowerPoints; we put posters on the walls about growth mindset. And then we close the art room because it is cheaper to buy textbooks than paint.

I am not asking for more funding. I am asking for the funding we already have to be spent honestly — on the subjects that change lives, not just the ones that appear in league tables.

If I Could Change One Thing About This School

Every school has its flaws — the question is whether anyone bothers to fix them. At Riverside Academy, there is one problem that affects every student, every day, and costs nothing to solve: the way we use tutor time.

Twenty minutes every morning, five days a week, forty weeks a year. That is over sixty-six hours of tutor time per year. And what do we do with it? We sit in silence while the register is taken. We watch a motivational video that nobody listens to. We are told about events that could have been covered in an email.

Imagine if those sixty-six hours were used differently. Imagine silent reading on Mondays — actual reading, not staring at a phone hidden inside a book. Imagine debate sessions on Wednesdays where students practise speaking in front of others. Imagine Friday tutorials where tutors help with GCSE revision, one subject at a time, across the whole year group.

The infrastructure already exists. The time is already allocated. The rooms are already booked. The only thing missing is the willingness to use them better.

This is not a radical proposal. It is a practical one. And it would cost the school nothing except the courage to admit that what we are doing right now is a waste of time.

Good morning.

I want you to do something. Think about the last thing you searched on your phone. Now imagine your teacher reading it out loud to the class. Uncomfortable? Good. Because that is roughly the level of privacy you actually have online.

Every search you make, every link you click, every message you type is being collected, stored, and sold — not to protect you, but to profit from you. You are not the customer of these platforms. You are the product. And the companies selling you have decided that your data is worth more than your dignity.

Some people say privacy does not matter if you have nothing to hide. This is the most dangerous sentence in the English language. Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing. It is about preserving the right to think, to explore, to make mistakes, and to change your mind — without a permanent digital record that follows you into adulthood.

Consider this: a thirteen-year-old who googles a question about their mental health today may find that search used against them by an insurance company in fifteen years. A teenager who posts a political opinion may have it weaponised during a job interview decades later. We are creating a world in which growing up is no longer allowed to be private.

I am not asking you to delete your accounts. I am asking you to understand what you are giving away. Because the first step to protecting your privacy is knowing you have already lost it.

passages.text:
Dear Secretary of State,

I am writing as a sixteen-year-old student who will sit eight GCSE examinations this summer. I do not write to complain about the difficulty of these exams, nor to request that they be made easier. I write to question whether the system that produces them is still fit for purpose.

The current examination model was designed for a world in which knowledge was scarce and memorisation was valuable. That world no longer exists. A student today carries more information in their pocket than the Library of Alexandria contained in its entirety. The question is no longer whether students can remember facts — it is whether they can think critically, communicate effectively, and solve problems that do not yet have answers.

I am not suggesting that knowledge does not matter. It does. But a system that allocates seventy per cent of its marks to a two-hour written exam under timed conditions is testing memory and exam technique — not understanding, not creativity, not resilience, and not the skills that employers consistently say graduates lack.

You may argue that examinations provide rigour and fairness. I agree. But rigour is not the same as relevance. A system can be rigorous and still prepare students for a world that no longer exists. The question is not whether exams should be abolished — they should not — but whether they should be the only measure of a student's worth.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss these concerns with your department. I suspect you would find that the students sitting these exams have rather more insight into their limitations than the adults who designed them.

Yours faithfully,
Sarah Mbeki
